description: We're two students with a shared interest in space, technology and trying out new ideas. We love the thought of exploring what life beyond Earth could look like, and we're excited to turn that curiosity into something interactive. For this challenge, we're working on a lunar outpost simulation where players get to make decisions, manage resources and experience some of the challenges astronauts might face. We're here to learn, experiment and have fun building something meaningful!
summary:
Moonbase: Outpost Zero is a browser game where you play a junior astronaut looking after a small lunar outpost. Over three short chapters you work out why the power keeps flickering, clean dust off the solar panels, and decide how to prepare for a solar storm.
What we care about most is that nothing happens in isolation. Dusty panels mean less power. Less power means the air scrubber and water recycler struggle, and plants stop growing. There’s a lunar night when the panels make nothing, so the battery has to carry the base. Shelter walls can be built from Moon soil or from water, but water spent on walls is water the crew can’t drink. When something goes wrong, the game tells you why.
You can also find ten lunar samples, from basalt and breccia to orange volcanic glass, evidence of polar water ice, and Neil Armstrong’s first footprint. Each one opens in a 2D viewer you can rotate and zoom, with a short quiz.
It runs offline, with an optional NASA space-weather feed. All the numbers are simplified for learning, and it isn’t a real simulator or endorsed by NASA. We haven’t yet tested it with real players or on real phones.
details:
1. What does the project do?

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational game that introduces players to the challenges of operating a space outpost. Players take on the role of astronauts, investigate problems, manage limited resources, and make decisions that affect the success of their missions. The game aims to make space science easier to understand through practical, decision-based activities rather than just theoretical explanations.

2. How does it work?

The game follows a mission-based structure with three chapters:

  • Chapter 1 – Power Flicker: Players investigate power-related problems and complete activities involving electrical systems, life support, plant bays, and shelter.
  • Chapter 2 – Dust on the Solar Farm: Players respond to a lunar dust storm warning, examine sensor information, and choose suitable preparation strategies.
  • Chapter 3 – The Repair Plan: Players match scientific clues to station systems, manage a power budget, and select repair strategies.

3. Benefits

  • Makes space science more engaging and interactive.
  • Introduces the importance of life-support systems and resource management.
  • Develops critical thinking and logical reasoning.
  • Encourages problem-solving and decision-making.
  • Helps players understand that different systems in a space habitat depend on one another.

4. Intended Impact

Our goal is to encourage curiosity about space exploration, especially among younger learners. We want players to understand that living beyond Earth involves more than travelling into space: astronauts must also maintain essential systems, conserve resources, prepare for environmental challenges, and make informed decisions.

The project aims to make these concepts accessible through an enjoyable learning experience.

5. What tools were used?

  • Visual Studio Code – for writing and editing the code.
  • Web browser – for running and testing the game.
  • Netlify – for hosting and sharing the playable project.
  • AI-assisted coding tools – if applicable, for development support and debugging.

6. Coding languages

  • HTML – structures the game and its content.
  • CSS – controls the visual design, layout, and styling.
  • JavaScript – handles gameplay, interactions, mission logic, and decision-making.

7. Hardware requirements

No specialised hardware is required.

8. Software requirements

  • A modern web browser.
  • Internet access for the hosted version.
  • Visual Studio Code for development and editing.

9. How is it creative?

Instead of presenting space science as a collection of facts, our project turns it into an interactive mission experience.

The game also connects several space-related concepts, such as electrical power, life support, lunar dust, plant systems, and habitat protection, within one experience.

10. What factors did we consider?

While developing the project, we considered:

  • Educational value: Scientific concepts should be understandable to younger learners.
  • Scientific relevance: Missions should introduce challenges associated with maintaining a space habitat.
  • Resource management: Players should understand the importance of balancing limited resources.
  • Decision-making: Choices should have meaningful consequences within the game.
  • Accessibility: The game should be easy to access through a web browser without specialised equipment.
  • User experience: Instructions, interactions, and mission objectives should be easy to follow.
  • Feasibility: The project should be achievable using beginner-friendly web technologies.
  • Engagement: The missions should encourage exploration, experimentation, and replaying to learn from different decisions.

Overall, our project combines space science, interactive storytelling, and decision-based gameplay to create an accessible introduction to the challenges of human space exploration.
